subject: circuits

milestone.title: Ohm's law and power
milestone.objective: Compute voltage, current, resistance and power for a single resistor, with units, in under 2 minutes per problem

sources.title: Course notes p.3 (fixture)
sources.text: Ohm's law: V = I R, where V is the voltage across the resistor in volts (V), I the current through it in amperes (A) and R the resistance in ohms. The power dissipated by a resistor is P = V I. Substituting Ohm's law gives P = I^2 R = V^2 / R. Power is measured in watts (W). Example: a current of 2 A through a 10 ohm resistor gives V = 2 x 10 = 20 V and P = 2^2 x 10 = 40 W. Example: 12 V across a 6 ohm resistor gives I = 12 / 6 = 2 A and P = 12^2 / 6 = 24 W.

lesson_lines: **V = I R**: voltage across the resistor (V) equals current through it (A) times its resistance (Ω). Rearranged: I = V / R and R = V / I.
A resistor turns electrical power into heat: **P = V I**. With Ohm's law you get two more forms: P = I² R and P = V² / R. Power is in watts (W).
Example: 2 A through 10 Ω. Then V = 2 × 10 = 20 V and P = 2² × 10 = 20 W.
Example: 12 V across 6 Ω. Then I = 12 / 6 = 2 A and P = 12² / 6 = 24 W.
Pick the power formula that uses the two quantities you already know. Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles the power it dissipates.
Solve: 9 V across 450 Ω. Find I and P, with units.

planted_errors.quote: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor doubles the power it dissipates.
planted_errors.correct: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor quadruples the power (P = V²/R).
planted_errors.why: Planted in a [Source: model] section: tests the own-knowledge check. P = V²/R, so 2V gives 4P.
